title: Common Medical Conditions: Asthma & Diabetes
description: Causes, symptoms and management of asthma and diabetes (Type 1, Type 2, hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia) in sport.
content_html:
Medical Conditions in Sport

Many sports performers live with long-term medical conditions. Asthma and diabetes are two of the most common conditions encountered in sport. Understanding their causes, symptoms and management is essential for coaches, teachers and performers so that participation can continue safely and emergencies can be handled correctly.

Asthma: Causes and Triggers

Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition in which the airways become inflamed, narrow and produce excess mucus, making breathing difficult. The exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but two key triggers are especially relevant in sport. Environmental triggers include cold air, air pollution, pollen, dust, pet dander and cigarette smoke — all of which can inflame the airways. Exercise is a particularly important trigger: during vigorous physical activity, increased ventilation draws cold, dry air deep into the airways, which can provoke an asthma attack — sometimes called exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

Asthma: Symptoms and Treatment

The four key symptoms of asthma are: coughing (often worse at night or after exercise), wheezing (a whistling or rattling sound on breathing out), shortness of breath (difficulty getting enough air, particularly during exertion) and tightness in the chest (a squeezing feeling that can feel like pressure). During an asthma attack all four symptoms may occur together and can escalate rapidly.

Treatment in a sporting context has two elements: reassurance — remaining calm, helping the performer sit upright in a position that opens the chest, and reassuring them reduces anxiety, which otherwise worsens the attack; and inhalers or nebulisers — a reliever inhaler (usually blue) delivers bronchodilator medication (typically salbutamol) that relaxes the airway muscles and opens the airways within minutes. A nebuliser delivers the same medication as a fine mist for more severe cases. If a performer's reliever inhaler does not work after 10 puffs, or if they become very distressed or their lips turn blue, call 999 immediately.

Key Fact

The four symptoms of asthma are coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and tightness in the chest. Treatment involves reassurance and a reliever inhaler (or nebuliser). If the inhaler fails after 10 puffs, call 999 immediately.

Diabetes: Type 1 and Type 2

Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot regulate insulin correctly, leading to abnormal blood sugar levels. There are two main types. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition typically diagnosed in childhood or young adulthood — the body's immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, so the body produces no insulin at all and the person is entirely dependent on insulin injections or a pump. Type 2 diabetes is much more common and is strongly linked to lifestyle factors such as a poor diet and physical inactivity; the body either does not produce enough insulin or the cells become resistant to it. Type 2 is more commonly diagnosed in adults, though increasing numbers of young people are affected.

Diabetes: Symptoms and Treatment

Common symptoms of both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes include: increased thirst (the body tries to dilute excess blood sugar by drawing water from cells), urinating more often (kidneys filter excess glucose through urine), extreme tiredness (cells cannot access glucose for energy), unexplained weight loss and cuts or wounds that take a long time to heal (high blood sugar impairs immune function and circulation). These symptoms are shared across both types, though Type 1 tends to develop more rapidly.

Treatment differs by type: Type 1 requires daily insulin injections or an insulin pump, as well as careful diet management. Type 2 is often managed initially through lifestyle changes — including increased physical activity and a healthier diet — with medication or insulin added if lifestyle changes are insufficient. Both types require regular blood sugar monitoring, especially around exercise, as physical activity significantly affects blood glucose levels.

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: the body cannot produce insulin (autoimmune). Type 2 diabetes: the body does not produce enough insulin or insulin does not work properly (lifestyle-linked). Both types share the same five common symptoms.

Blood Sugar Levels: Hypos and Hyperglycaemia

Blood sugar levels in a diabetic performer can fall dangerously low or rise dangerously high, both of which are medical emergencies. Hypoglycaemia (a 'hypo') occurs when blood sugar falls too low — often triggered by exercise, missed meals or too much insulin. Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, pallor and weakness. Treatment is rapid ingestion of fast-acting glucose (e.g. glucose tablets, a sugary drink or orange juice). Exercise significantly increases the risk of a hypo in Type 1 diabetics, so blood sugar should be checked before, during and after activity. Hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar) develops more slowly — caused by too little insulin, too many carbohydrates or illness — and symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination and fatigue. Severe hyperglycaemia requires medical attention.

A performer with asthma should always have their reliever inhaler immediately accessible during sport — not locked away in a bag or locker. A thorough warm-up is especially important because it gradually raises ventilation rather than shocking the airways with sudden intense effort. In cold weather, wearing a scarf or sports buff over the mouth and nose warms and humidifies the inhaled air, reducing the exercise-induced trigger. Coaches should know which performers have asthma, where their inhalers are kept, and the action to take if an attack occurs.

A Type 1 diabetic performer should check blood glucose before exercise and have fast-acting carbohydrates (e.g. glucose tablets or a sports drink) immediately to hand during activity. If blood sugar is low before training, a carbohydrate snack should be eaten and glucose rechecked before starting. Exercise generally lowers blood sugar, so insulin doses may need adjusting on training days — this should always be done in consultation with a medical professional. Coaches should know the signs of a hypo and have access to glucose sources at the venue.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about diabetes, be precise about the cause: Type 1 is 'the body cannot produce insulin' and Type 2 is 'the body does not produce enough insulin or the insulin does not work properly'. Do not say Type 2 is simply 'diet-related' — this is too vague. For hypoglycaemia questions, state the treatment as 'fast-acting glucose / a sugary drink', not just 'eat something'. Accuracy on medical conditions is directly linked to marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Asthma symptoms are coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest tightness; treatment is reassurance plus a reliever inhaler, with 999 called if the inhaler fails after 10 puffs.
  • Type 1 diabetes means the body cannot produce insulin; Type 2 means it does not produce enough or insulin does not work properly; both share symptoms of increased thirst, frequent urination, extreme tiredness, weight loss and slow-healing cuts.
  • Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) is treated with fast-acting glucose and is a particular risk during exercise; hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar) develops more slowly and requires medical attention if severe.

glossary_terms.definition: Conditions that affect normal body function over a prolonged period and may require ongoing management, particularly during physical activity.
A sudden worsening of asthma symptoms caused by airway narrowing, making it very difficult to breathe.
A hormone produced by the pancreas that allows cells to absorb glucose from the blood and use it for energy.
A condition where blood sugar falls below the normal range, causing symptoms such as shakiness, sweating, confusion and weakness.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a symptom of asthma?
A) Increased thirst
B) Wheezing
C) Slow-healing cuts
D) Extreme tiredness
State two differences between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Type 1 — body cannot produce insulin; Type 2 — body does not produce enough insulin or insulin does not work properly. Type 1 — typically diagnosed in childhood/young adulthood; Type 2 — more commonly diagnosed in adults. Type 1 — autoimmune cause; Type 2 — strongly linked to lifestyle factors such as poor diet and physical inactivity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what hypoglycaemia is and how it should be treated during a sports session.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Definition (1 mark): hypoglycaemia is when blood sugar falls below the normal range / is dangerously low. Symptoms (1 mark): symptoms include shakiness, sweating, dizziness or confusion. Treatment (1 mark): treat immediately with fast-acting glucose — e.g. glucose tablets or a sugary drink — and stop the activity until blood sugar returns to a safe level. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a coach should manage a performer who has an asthma attack during a training session. Give an example of what the coach should do if the inhaler does not work.
practice_questions.marks: Management (up to 3 marks): stop the activity and ensure the performer sits upright (1 mark); provide reassurance to reduce anxiety (1 mark); help the performer use their reliever inhaler — up to 10 puffs, one puff every 30 to 60 seconds (1 mark). Example of inhaler failure (1 mark): if symptoms do not improve after 10 puffs of the inhaler, or if the performer becomes very distressed or their lips turn blue, call 999 immediately. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A gymnastics coach has two performers in her squad: one has asthma and one has Type 1 diabetes. Both conditions can affect performance and safety during training.

Discuss the measures the coach should take to manage both conditions safely during a gymnastics training session.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A structured discussion of measures for both conditions. Asthma: confirm inhaler is accessible, ensure thorough warm-up, recognise symptoms and treatment protocol. Diabetes: pre-session blood glucose check, fast-acting carbohydrates available, signs of a hypo, communication with performer about their management plan. At least one contrasting point — e.g. the coach can take all the right steps, but the performer themselves must also take responsibility for managing their condition. Some comparison or discussion of both conditions' impact on session design.
Secure (3–4 marks): Measures for both conditions identified and some explanation, with limited comparison.
Developing (2 marks): Measures for one condition only, or both mentioned but without detail.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point about either condition. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A secondary school PE department is considering whether students with asthma or diabetes should be allowed to participate in all physical activities without restriction.

Evaluate the extent to which students with asthma or diabetes should be included in all physical activities, and what measures are needed to make this safe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing for inclusion (physical activity has proven benefits for both conditions — exercise improves lung function over time in asthma; regular activity improves insulin sensitivity and blood glucose control in Type 2 diabetes) contrasted with realistic risks (exercise triggers asthma attacks; exercise lowers blood sugar and can cause dangerous hypos in Type 1 diabetics). Specific measures are then evaluated (inhaler on site, blood sugar checks, warm-up protocols, emergency plans) and a judgement reached — e.g. that full inclusion is the right approach when appropriate management protocols are in place, but blanket inclusion without individual risk assessment is not responsible.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments for and against explored, measures described, partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists measures with limited evaluation or judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the correct description of the cause of Type 1 diabetes?
options: The body produces too much insulin
The body does not produce enough insulin or insulin does not work properly
The body cannot absorb glucose from food

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed symptom of asthma?
During exercise, a Type 1 diabetic performer is most at risk of _____, which occurs when blood sugar falls dangerously low.
The treatment for an asthma attack in sport is reassurance and a reliever _____, which delivers bronchodilator medication to open the airways.
Match each condition to its primary management strategy during sport.
right: Fast-acting glucose such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink
Lifestyle changes including increased physical activity and healthier diet
Reliever inhaler plus reassurance; call 999 if no improvement after 10 puffs

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four symptoms of asthma?
flashcard_questions.a: Coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and tightness in the chest are the four symptoms listed in the specification.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes an asthma attack during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Increased ventilation during exercise draws cold, dry air into the airways, causing inflammation and narrowing known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

flashcard_questions.q: What should a coach do if a performer's reliever inhaler has not worked after 10 puffs?
flashcard_questions.a: The coach should call 999 immediately, as the asthma attack is severe and requires emergency medical attention.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference in insulin production between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Type 1: the body cannot produce insulin at all. Type 2: the body does not produce enough insulin, or the insulin produced does not work properly.

flashcard_questions.q: State two lifestyle factors linked to the development of Type 2 diabetes.
flashcard_questions.a: Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to a poor diet and physical inactivity, both of which contribute to insulin resistance over time.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five common symptoms shared by Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Increased thirst, urinating more often, extreme tiredness, unexplained weight loss, and cuts that take a long time to heal.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hypoglycaemia and what causes it during a sports session?
flashcard_questions.a: Hypoglycaemia is dangerously low blood sugar, most often triggered during sport by exercise using up blood glucose faster than it is replaced.

flashcard_questions.q: How should a hypoglycaemic episode be treated immediately?
flashcard_questions.a: The performer should stop activity and consume fast-acting glucose immediately, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should a performer with asthma carry out a thorough warm-up before intense exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: A gradual warm-up raises ventilation slowly, reducing the shock of cold dry air to the airways and lowering the risk of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does exercise lower blood sugar in a Type 1 diabetic performer?
flashcard_questions.a: Working muscles absorb glucose from the blood for energy during exercise, causing blood sugar levels to drop, which can lead to a hypo.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hyperglycaemia and how does it differ from hypoglycaemia?
flashcard_questions.a: Hyperglycaemia is high blood sugar (caused by too little insulin or too many carbohydrates), whereas hypoglycaemia is dangerously low blood sugar.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a nebuliser do, and when might it be used instead of an inhaler?
flashcard_questions.a: A nebuliser converts medication into a fine mist for inhalation, used in severe asthma attacks when a standard inhaler cannot deliver sufficient medication.
